==Problem==
Five different awards are to be given to three students. Each student will receive at least one award. In how many different ways can the awards be distributed? 

<math>\textbf{(A) }120 \qquad \textbf{(B) }150 \qquad \textbf{(C) }180 \qquad \textbf{(D) }210 \qquad \textbf{(E) }240</math>

==Solution 1 (Constructive Counting)==
Firstly, observe that a single student can't receive <imath>4</imath> or <imath>5</imath> awards because this would mean that one of the other students receives no awards. Thus, each student must receive either <imath>1</imath>, <imath>2</imath>, or <imath>3</imath> awards. If a student receives <imath>3</imath> awards, then the other two students must each receive <imath>1</imath> award; if a student receives <imath>2</imath> awards, then another student must also receive <imath>2</imath> awards and the remaining student must receive <imath>1</imath> award. We consider each of these two cases in turn.

If a student receives three awards, there are <imath>3</imath> ways to choose which student this is, and <imath>\binom{5}{3}</imath> ways to give that student <imath>3</imath> out of the <imath>5</imath> awards. Next, there are <imath>2</imath> students left and <imath>2</imath> awards to give out, with each student getting one award. There are clearly just <imath>2</imath> ways to distribute these two awards out, giving <imath>3\cdot\binom{5}{3}\cdot 2=60</imath> ways to distribute the awards in this case.

In the other case, two students receive <imath>2</imath> awards and one student receives <imath>1</imath> award. We know there are <imath>3</imath> choices for which student gets <imath>1</imath> award. There are <imath>\binom{3}{1}</imath> ways to do this. Then, there are <imath>\binom{5}{2}</imath> ways to give the first student his two awards, leaving <imath>3</imath> awards yet to be distributed. There are then <imath>\binom{3}{2}</imath> ways to give the second student his <imath>2</imath> awards. Finally, there is only <imath>1</imath> student and <imath>1</imath> award left, so there is only <imath>1</imath> way to distribute this award. This results in <imath>\binom{5}{2}\cdot\binom{3}{2}\cdot 1\cdot 3 =90</imath> ways to distribute the awards in this case. Adding the results of these two cases, we get <imath>60+90=\boxed{\textbf{(B) }150}</imath>.

== Solution 2 (Version 2 of Solution 1) ==

Upon inspection (specified in the above solution), there are two cases of the distribution of awards to the students: one student gets 3 awards and the other each get 1 award or one student gets 1 award and the other two get 2 awards. 


In the first case, there are <imath>\binom{3}{1} = 3</imath> ways to choose the person who gets 3 awards. From here, there are <imath>\binom{5}{3} = 10</imath> ways to choose the 3 awards from the 5 total awards. Now, one person has <imath>2</imath> choices for awards and the other has <imath>1</imath> choice for the award. Thus, the total number of ways to choose awards in this case is <imath>3 \cdot 10 \cdot 2 \cdot 1 = 60</imath>.  


In the other case, there are <imath>\binom{3}{1} = 3</imath> ways to choose the person who gets 1 award, and <imath>5</imath> choices for his/her award. Then, one person has <imath>\binom{4}{2} = 6</imath> ways to have his/her awards and the other person has <imath>\dbinom{2}{2} = 1</imath> ways to have his/her awards. This gives <imath>3 \cdot 5 \cdot 6 \cdot 1  = 90</imath> ways for this case. 

Adding these numbers together, we get <imath>60 + 90 = 150</imath> ways to distribute the awards, or choice <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(B) }150}</imath>.

==Solution 3 (Complementary Counting)==

Without the restriction that each student receives at least one award, we could take each of the awards and choose one of the <math>3</math> students to give it to. This would be <math>3^5</math> ways to distribute the awards in total. Now we need to subtract the cases where at least one student doesn't receive an award. If a student doesn't receive an award, there are <math>3</math> choices for which student that is, so <math>2^5</math> ways of choosing a student to receive each of the awards; in total, <math>3\cdot32=96</math>.

However, if <math>2</math> students both don't receive an award, then this case would be counted twice among the <math>96</math>, so we need to add back in these cases. Said in other words, <math>2</math> students not receiving an award is equivalent to <math>1</math> student receiving <math>5</math> awards, and there are <math>3</math> choices for whom that student would be. To finish, the total number of ways to distribute the awards is <math>243 - 96+3</math>, or <math>\boxed{\textbf{(B) }150}</math>.
